extracted.intended_audience: government contracting officers, government legal counsel, sureties, and contractors involved in U.S. federal contracts
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of administrative and judicial standards governing U.S. Government contracts: bond obligations, surety rights, annulment/default, options, delivery/quantity adjustments, labor restrictions, and related procurement issues, illustrated by authorities and example holdings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surety obligation does not create equitable lien against United States (XX C 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: The new obligation of the surety under the act of August 13, 1894 (28 Stat. 278) does not create an additional obligation on the part of the United States in the nature of an equitable lien or other right against the United States; the United States has no right to withhold funds due a contractor for the purpose of indemnifying a surety for moneys paid out by him to material men and laborers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withholding payments due a contractor to indemnify a surety would be an assumption by the United States to insure payments that the contract and bond are intended to secure, and would improperly oblige disbursing officers to adjudicate contractor-creditor disputes. Even where a surety obtains a state-court injunction against the contractor, the United States may not withhold payments at the request of the surety. (Citations: multiple departmental opinions: C. 7311, Nov. 21, 1899; C. 20021, July 10, 1906; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Modification of contract without surety consent does not release obligation to labor/material-men (XX C 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract was modified by supplemental agreement without the consent of the surety on the contractor's bond, the contractor's bond may be considered as having two obligations (one to secure due performance to the United States and one to secure payment to labor and material-men on behalf of them), and the obligation for the benefit of labor and material-men was not released by modification without surety consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the bond as potentially bifurcated; absence of surety consent to modification does not necessarily discharge the bond's protection of third-party suppliers. (C. 17474, Feb. 3, 1905.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionable applicability of bond requirement to municipal instrumentalities (XX C 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the United States contracts with a municipal instrumentality (e.g., board of water commissioners of a city) for work to supply a Government post, it may be doubtful whether such contracts are within the true intent of the act of August 13, 1894 (28 Stat. 278), and it may be recommended that no bond be exacted for protection of persons supplying labor and materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the character of the contracting party; bonds required by statute for private contractors may not be appropriate or required for municipal entities — exercise discretion and obtain legal advice. (C. 25610, Sept. 24, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: War Department may not delist surety to compel settlement of subcontractor claims (XX C 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where principal and surety failed to pay a subcontractor and the subcontractor requested the War Department strike the surety from its acceptable list to compel settlement, such action was outside the duty of the War Department under the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative de-listing to pressure sureties is not an authorized remedy under the statute; subcontractors should pursue statutorily provided remedies. (G. 10553, June 4, 1901.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of bankrupt sale on original contractor's performance bond and labor/material bond (XX C 10 & XX C 11 first)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Government contractor goes into bankruptcy and the purchaser under a bankrupt sale of the contractor's contract rights is permitted to carry out the Government contract, the bond given by the original contractor conditioned for faithful performance by the original contractor will continue in force and sureties remain liable for damages from the original contractor's failure to perform. However, the bond given to protect labor and material-men is limited by its terms to labor and material supplied to the original contractor and would not continue as such in favor of a subsequent purchaser; the purchaser should furnish a new bond to secure labor and material-men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize distinction between performance bond (may remain operative as to Government's remedies) and statutory labor/material bond (protections may be limited to original contractor). Purchaser of contract rights normally must provide a new bond to protect suppliers. (U. S. v. cases cited; U. 23265, Oct. 30, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Surety undertaking completion in its own name must give bond to protect labor/material-men (XX C 11 second)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contractor defaulted and a supplemental agreement terminated the original contract and the surety undertook the work in its own name, such surety should give a bond to protect labor and material-men as required by the act of August 13, 1894 (28 Stat. 278).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A surety that steps in as principal (to complete work) must comply with statutory bond requirements protecting suppliers; do not assume original bond suffices when surety becomes performing party. (O. 18079, Oct. 1, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppliers to subcontractors — certified copy of contract and bond upon affidavit (XX C 12)
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of August 13, 1894 is believed to protect persons furnishing labor or materials to subcontractors as well as to the original contractor; a party who has furnished material to a subcontractor should be given a certified copy of the contract and bond upon filing the affidavit required by the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When suppliers to subcontractors file the statutory affidavit, supply authenticated copies of contract and bond for their use in pursuing claims; courts may ultimately decide scope but administrative practice favors providing copies. (G. 1908, Jan. 4, 1896.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No payment until statutorily required bond is filed (XX C 13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a contractor completes work but fails to furnish the bond required by the act of August 13, 1894 for protection of persons supplying labor and materials, no payments should be made until such bond is filed; this rule applies to an assignee as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce bond-filing requirement as condition precedent to payments; ensure proposed bonds are properly executed before disbursing funds. (C. 4082, May 3, 1898.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Certified copy of contract and bond should be authenticated under Department seal (XX C 14)
rubrics_metrics.description: The certified copy of the contract and bond furnished under the act should, in accordance with section 882, R. S., be authenticated under the seal of the War Department so such copy is proper form for use as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow formal authentication procedures (departmental seal) when issuing certified copies to third parties to ensure admissibility and proper evidentiary form. (C. 1743, Sept. 24, 1895.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient of certified contract and bond may institute suit without Secretary permission (XX C 15)
rubrics_metrics.description: A duly certified copy of the contract and bond furnished under the act having been furnished, the party furnished with a copy may institute suit as provided therein and it is not necessary for him first to obtain the permission of the Secretary of War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-party beneficiaries who obtain certified copies and meet statutory prerequisites may bring suit directly; administrative permission is not a prerequisite. (C. 2319, May 25, 1896.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracting officer must take positive action to annul; mere delay not automatic forfeiture (XXI A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract provided that upon failure to prosecute faithfully and diligently the contracting officer could annul the contract and forfeiture of retained percentages would follow, mere failure to deliver within the time named did not operate as an automatic forfeiture; there must be positive action by the contracting officer indicating intention to annul and such intention should be communicated to the contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annulment requires affirmative steps and notice; do not treat late performance as automatic termination absent express contractual automatic-forfeiture language and communicated intent. (P. 34, 229, Aug. 2, 1889.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Breach of a term does not ordinarily authorize annulment without express covenant (XXI B)
rubrics_metrics.description: A breach such as failure to deliver some articles at the agreed time will not ordinarily, in the absence of an express covenant to that effect, authorize the Secretary of War to declare the contract annulled; rather the United States has a right of action for damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between remedies: damages versus annulment — seek express contract language before treating breaches as grounds for annulment. (P. 29, 324; 34, 261.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Annulment carried out in accordance with terms is final (XXI C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract was regularly annulled in accordance with its terms, that action of annulment was final and could not be rescinded so as to revive the contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once properly annulled per contract terms, the contract cannot be later revived by administrative rescission of the annulment — treat finality seriously. (C. 7931, Apr. 7, 1900.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Government taking possession under annulment treated as purchase; revalue plant and account for depreciation (XXI D)
rubrics_metrics.description: When contract provided for Government completion upon default and that Government should take possession of materials, tools, buildings, etc., and Government took possession, the taking was treated as by way of purchase; for final settlement, plant should be revalued with credit for depreciation from its use; plant may be used on other works with proper credit to original appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In default completions where Government takes contractor property, perform fair revaluation, account for depreciation, and credit appropriations when reusing plant. (C. 27890, Mar. 6, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: To annul for delay there must be substantial failure to prosecute faithfully and diligently (XXII A / XXII B)
rubrics_metrics.description: An unreasonable delay to commence delivery may indicate abandonment and justify treating the contract as relinquished; sustained failure to make satisfactory progress, provide information, or maintain a business presence may indicate repudiation, justifying contracting-office steps to supply deficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate facts of delay/progress; isolated or excusable delays may not equal abandonment — documented, substantial nonperformance or movement away from business are strong grounds for early remedial action. (P. 29, 324; C. 24639, Mar. 27, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No authority to insert citizenship/employment restrictions into Government contracts absent statute (XXIII A / E / G)
rubrics_metrics.description: It was held that there was no law authorizing insertion of clauses prohibiting employment of non-citizens or restricting bidders to citizens; absent a statute restricting purchase to domestic production or produced by American labor only, there is no authority to restrict contracts by executive regulation; statutes that prefer American material leave discretion to Secretary to procure elsewhere when justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not impose nationality-based bidder or employment restrictions unless statutory authority exists; where statute provides preference (e.g., to American manufacture), Secretary retains discretion to authorize exceptions under justifying conditions. (C. 16057; C. 18209; C. 29307, Dec. 14, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary lacks general power to control contractor's labor absent statute (XXIII B)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of statutory regulation, the Secretary of War is not empowered to exercise control over the labor employed by contractors (e.g., on jetties) or to prevent their availing themselves of convict labor lawfully hired out by states; federal enforcement of state criminal statutes is not under the Secretary’s administrative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt administrative policing of contractor labor composition without legislative backing; criminal statutes are executed through ordinary criminal processes, not contracting control. (P. 48, 402; C. 3542.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive order restricting convict labor is strictly construed as limiting contract 'employment of labor' (XXIII D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive order May 18, 1905 forbids employment of persons undergoing sentences of imprisonment at hard labor in contract performance; the order restricts freedom of contract and should be strictly construed — it may not apply to articles procured in the open market (e.g., bricks) but does apply where contract contemplates quarrying, delivery, or manufacturing (i.e., direct employment of labor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using executive-order restrictions, analyze whether the contract contemplates employment of labor vs. purchase of goods; apply strict construction. Examples: quarrying/delivery, laundering, manufacturing per specification are 'employment of labor' (C. 20668; C. 18102; C. 18831).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect procurement from sources using convict labor does not necessarily violate contract prohibition (XXIII F)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract prohibited employment of convict labor, but contractor procured coal from a seller who bought it from a State that used convict labor in mining, the contractor would not necessarily be violating the contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish direct employment in contract performance from indirect market procurement; prohibitions aimed at direct employment may not reach market supply chains absent express language. (C. 23652, July 27, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory appropriation may condition purchase on American manufacture but allows Secretary's limited discretion for foreign purchases (XXIII H)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortification appropriations declared material purchased under the act should be of American manufacture, except when Secretary of War in his judgment finds it manifestly in the national interest to make limited purchases abroad (duty-free). The Secretary may in exercise of that discretion issue general authorizations under proper conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriation statutes include domestic-manufacture requirements with exceptions, apply Secretary’s discretionary standards and document conditions for foreign procurement. (C. 29307, Dec. 14, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Government option elections on quantities are binding and limit later changes (XXIV — variations and options)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a contract specified approximate quantities subject to variation (e.g., ±10%) and the Government elected the minimum (or a specified increase), the Government was bound by that election and could not subsequently require the opposite election (e.g., later require the maximum). Similarly, an exercised option to increase by a stated percentage (e.g., 20%) where no reservation for further increases existed precludes further increases absent contractual reservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Government choices about optional increases or reductions as binding elections once communicated and acted upon; do not retroactively change options. Examples: dredging quantities reduced 10% and later attempted increase was invalid (C. 21308); cloth increase of 20% exercised could not be further increased absent reservation (C. 22676).

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment and final settlement interactions with option increases and retained percentages (XXIV — final voucher / estoppel)
rubrics_metrics.description: A chief quartermaster’s payment in full and marking a voucher 'contract completed' is not a legal release (no consideration) of future option obligations, but if the contractor was disadvantaged thereby (failed to hold supplies) the Government may be estopped from later calling for additional quantity. A 50% increase ordered may be treated as continuing the contract so final settlement (and retained percentages) awaits completion of increased quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when making payments/marking vouchers before options are exercised or while options remain outstanding; administrative acts may create equitable estoppel if contractor reasonably relies and is disadvantaged. Retained percentages generally remain until final settlement including any exercised increases. (C. 12974; C. 22420.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Government must exercise options within contract duration and allow reasonable delivery time (XXIV — timing and reasonable time)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the contract's option to increase quantity is limited 'during the continuance of this contract,' the contractor cannot be required after the contract expiration date to furnish increased quantity. Where no delivery time for ordered additional quantity is specified, contractor is entitled to a reasonable time to make deliveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check contract term and explicit time limits for option exercise; when silent, supply reasonable delivery periods consistent with practical production/delivery constraints. (C. 21676; C. 26826.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Option clauses applying to periodic deliveries are applied to total quantity unless language treats each period separately (XXIV — monthly deliveries)
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract providing monthly deliveries and an overall 20% increase option will not, absent clear language, be construed so that the 20% applies to each monthly installment separately; the option may be applied to overall quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret aggregate option language in context; avoid reading periodic-schedule contracts as separately optioned each period unless expressly provided. (C. 27506, Nov. 22, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: United States occupies leased premises with implied covenant to avoid unnecessary injury (XXV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the United States occupies premises under an express or implied contract to pay rent, an implied obligation arises to use the premises so as not to injure them unnecessarily; the United States is liable for damages to buildings, fences, or crops resulting from such use and the officer charged may liquidate damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat occupancy as tenancy with implied duties of care; document and compensate for damages where appropriate. (C. 14971; C. 14617; C. 144^^.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Representations concerning accessibility can be warranties (XXVI)
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract describing a point as 'accessible to boats propelled by steam or other power' when it is later discovered impossible for a steamer to approach within 75 miles of the point was a representation understood to be peculiarly within the Government's knowledge and should be treated as a warranty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When government descriptions involve matters within government knowledge, treat them as potential warranties; contractor relief may be available where the representation proves false. (C. 12705, Apr. 3, 1903.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Government may continue contractor insurance when it takes possession and charge expense to contractor (XXVII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract made contractor responsible for damage by fire and contractor insured to protect contractor and surety, and government took possession to complete work and charge excess cost to contractor, the Government could continue the insurance and charge expense to contractor as part of cost of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When government steps in and assumes custody, it may maintain necessary insurance protecting contractor interests and treat cost as chargeable to defaulting contractor in final accounting. (C. 21735, Feb. 18, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepted bidder's failure to enter contract: guarantors' liability and possibility of contracting with guarantor (unnumbered P.32 authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an accepted bidder fails to enter into the contract, the liability of the guarantors attaches, and, where public interests are not prejudiced, the contract may lawfully be entered into with one of the guarantors as an open-market transaction in which the guarantor takes the risk on his own account at the bid rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When awardee fails to sign, treat guarantors' obligations under bid security seriously; consider contracting with guarantor only when lawful and in public interest. (P. 32, 188, May 4, 1889.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No obligation to give surety opportunity to perform unless provided in contract/bond (XXIX)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of a provision in the contract or accompanying bond requiring the Government to call upon the surety to carry out the contract in case of contractor default, the Government is under no obligation to give the surety such an opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume an implied duty to require surety performance; verify contract/bond language if Government intends to permit surety to complete performance. (C. 24639, Mar. 27, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Partnership dissolution before signing does not bar one partner from taking up the bid (XXX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the lowest bidder was a partnership and before the contract could be signed the partnership was dissolved, there is no legal objection to allowing one member of the former partnership to take up the bid and enter into the contract (effectively rejecting and re-making contract with that member).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administratively, permits flexibility to contract with an individual partner post-dissolution, subject to fairness and public-interest considerations. (C. 12827, Sept. 10, 1902.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Payments to partners may be made to any member despite protest (XXXI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Payments due on a contract where contractors are partners may legally be made to any member of the firm, notwithstanding one partner has filed a protest and notice against payment to a partner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect Government by allowing payment to any partner; internal partner disputes are not ordinarily binding on Government unless statutory or contractual reason exists. (C. 3210, May 20, 1897.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Army Regulations not strictly applicable to independent boards but may be followed (XXXII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Army Regulations are not strictly applicable to contracts of the United States Soldiers' Home, which is under control of a board of commissioners empowered to establish regulations, but Army Regulations provide comprehensive instructions that may wisely be followed except where board prescribes different regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Army Regulations as persuasive guidance for contracting entities under separate governance, while respecting the separate authority of boards or statutory bodies. (C. 19921, June 16, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee contract requiring notice and forfeiture of pay for early quitting is reasonable (XXXIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed contract where an employee promised not to leave service without consent and to give 50 days' notice, with forfeiture of pay if violated, was held not unreasonable or oppressive and had no legal objection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court/administrative acceptance of notice-and-forfeiture clauses may be permissible if reasonable in scope and not unduly oppressive; such provisions can be used to protect continuity of specialized government services. (C. 23026, Apr. 3, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Government inviting bids does not necessarily abandon option to renew (XXXIV)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Government contract giving an option to renew year-to-year; toward the close of the fiscal year the Government advertised for bids for the next year. This invitation for bids did not constitute abandonment of its option to renew, but was a means of ascertaining whether it would be in the interest of the United States to exercise the option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative solicitation of competing bids while holding an option is permissible and does not automatically waive the Government's renewal rights; document intent and exercise of option properly. (C. 28614, June 10, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract scope should be interpreted according to specified coverage (XXXV)
rubrics_metrics.description: A printing contract providing that the contractor should furnish printing and related supplies 'required at Headquarters Atlantic Division and Department of the East during the fiscal year' did not include printing for a constructing quartermaster in the department who was carrying on construction under Quartermaster General authority; the item was outside the contract's scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret contract scope narrowly according to specified beneficiaries and locations; avoid broad readings that expand obligations beyond expressly enumerated departments or offices. (C. 23212, July 7, 1908.)
